specAnchors.text: know the trends in solubility of the hydroxides and sulfates of Group 2 elements

primer.text: Two solubility arrows point in opposite directions down Group 2: hydroxides dissolve more readily as you descend, while sulfates become stubbornly insoluble. This note quantifies both trends from the data tables and connects hydroxide solubility to the growing alkalinity of oxide-water solutions.

modules.title: Hydroxide solubility and the alkalinity ladder
sourceHeadings: Solubility of the Group 2 Hydroxides Table
modules.opening: The oxide-water solutions grow more alkaline downward because the hydroxides themselves dissolve more readily. This lesson quantifies the ladder from Mg(OH)2's 2.0 x 10-5 up to Ba(OH)2's 1.5 x 10-2 moles per 100 g of water.
keyPoints: Dissolved oxides release hydroxide through O2- + H2O -> 2OH-.
The more hydroxide ions a solution holds, the more alkaline it is.
Alkalinity is therefore governed by hydroxide solubility.
Solubility climbs from Mg(OH)2 at 2.0 x 10-5 through Ca(OH)2 and Sr(OH)2 to Ba(OH)2 at 1.5 x 10-2.
Each hydroxide dissolves as X(OH)2 -> X2+ + 2OH-, doubling the ion yield per formula unit.

low.restatement: Solubility sets the hydroxide supply, and the hydroxide supply sets the pH - the table's climb from magnesium to barium is the alkalinity ladder in numbers.
low.analogy: Four taps dripping into one tank, each opening wider than the last: the water level (alkalinity) rises with the tap size (solubility).
low.examPointer: Quote at least two table values when asked to demonstrate the trend - one figure alone cannot show a climb.

medium.restatement: Each formula unit of X(OH)2 releases two OH- ions, so dissolved concentration maps directly onto pH; the 750-fold solubility span from magnesium to barium hydroxide compounds the doubling into a steeprise in alkalinity.
medium.analogy: A pay rise applied twice: first the wage (solubility) climbs, then each employee (formula unit) brings a plus-one (second hydroxide), compounding the household income.
medium.examPointer: The oxide trend and the hydroxide trend are one story - link them explicitly through the OH- concentration in explanations.

modules.title: Sulfate solubility and the Group 1 comparison
modules.opening: The sulfate arrow points the opposite way: solubility collapses down the group until barium sulfate barely dissolves at all. This lesson closes with the Group 1 comparison - why those compounds never precipitate and how barium hydroxide still loses to potassium hydroxide.
keyPoints: The solubility of Group 2 sulfates decreases going down the group.
Barium sulfate is effectively insoluble, the classic white precipitate.
Group 1 compounds are all soluble, so they never precipitate in cation tests.
Flame tests, not precipitation, identify Group 1 cations.
Even the most soluble Group 2 hydroxide, Ba(OH)2 at 4.68 g per 100 cm3, loses to KOH at 121 g.

low.restatement: Sulfates sink in solubility as you descend, Group 1 salts never sink at all, and even barium hydroxide's respectable figure cannot match potassium hydroxide's enormous one.
low.analogy: A water slide running the wrong way: Group 2 sulfates slide into shallower pools (less soluble) while Group 1 salts never leave the deep end.
low.examPointer: Bring the numbers: Ba(OH)2 at 4.68 g per 100 cm3 against KOH at 121 g - the comparison proves the 'increases down the group' claim is group-relative only.

medium.restatement: The sulfate descent means each step down trades solubility for lattice strength, ending at BaSO4's near-zero dissolution; the absence of any Group 1 precipitation follows from their universal solubility, which redirects cation testing to flame colours.
medium.analogy: Two opposite escalators in one mall: sulfates descend floor by floor until they stop at the basement (BaSO4), while Group 1 salts ride an up-only escalator with no exit.
medium.examPointer: Answer 'why no Group 1 trends' with 'all soluble, no precipitates, use flame tests' - the three-part answer earns all three marks.

glossary.definition: The increase in Group 2 hydroxide solubility from Mg(OH)2 down to Ba(OH)2 that drives the alkalinity ladder.
The decrease in Group 2 sulfate solubility down the group, bottoming out at insoluble barium sulfate.
The solid observation signalling an insoluble product, as in the barium sulfate test for sulfate ions.
